reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A USD 30m exposure has normally distributed one-period losses with mean +4.0% (an expected loss) and volatility 15.0%. For a normal, $ES = \mu + \sigma\,\phi(z)/(1-\alpha)$, with $z = 1.96$ and $\phi(1.96) = 0.0584$ at the 97.5% level.
ask: The 97.5% expected shortfall is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.5m
options.why: Used $\phi(z) = 0.0584$ directly as the tail multiplier and never divided by the 2.5% tail: $4\% + 15\% \times 0.0584 = 4.9\%$, about USD 1.5m.

options.label: ≈ USD 39m
options.why: Stopped at the percentage, 39.07%, and read it as USD millions without applying it to the USD 30m exposure.

options.label: ≈ USD 117m
options.why: Scale slip (10×): a decimal-place error when converting 39% of the exposure into dollars.

takeaway: The normal tail multiplier is $\phi(z)/(1-\alpha)$, about 2.34 at 97.5%. Divide by the tail probability, then scale to the exposure.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A process produces no loss 95% of the time. With probability 5% a loss occurs, and its size is normal with mean USD 4m and standard deviation USD 2m. Look at the 95% expected shortfall of the loss.
ask: Compared with USD 4m, the 95% ES is:

options.label: Well above USD 4m, about USD 8m
options.why: Applied the normal ES formula inside the severity distribution: $4 + 2\,\phi(1.645)/0.05 = 8.1$. That is the ES of the severity, not of the whole process.

options.label: Far below USD 4m, about USD 0.2m
options.why: Took the expected loss, $5\% \times 4 = 0.2$, instead of the average loss in the tail.

working.label: Tail mass
working.display: $1 - 0.95 = 5\%$, the same as the probability of a loss event

working.label: Tail contents
working.display: The worst 5% of outcomes are exactly the loss events

takeaway: When the tail mass equals the probability of the event, the tail average is just the mean severity. Do not run the normal ES formula on a mixed distribution.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A fund has 300 daily P/L observations. Its worst losses, in order, are 1.350, 1.000, 0.950, 0.920, 0.850, and so on down a list of 20. It estimates the 99% expected shortfall by averaging the tail losses.
ask: How many of the worst losses go into the 99% ES average?

options.why: Read the 1% tail as a single observation, so ES collapses to the worst loss of 1.350.
Averaged every loss in the listed table rather than the 1% tail.
Took a 10% tail (30 of 300), the wrong confidence level.

takeaway: Historical-simulation ES averages the worst $n(1-\alpha)$ observations. Here that is 3, so ES = 1.100.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A daily P/L distribution has a 2% chance of a USD 3 loss and an 8% chance of a USD 2 loss; everything else is a smaller loss or a gain. The 95% ES (relative to zero) averages the worst 5% of probability mass.
ask: How much probability from the USD 2 loss outcome falls inside the worst 5% tail?

options.why: Took the whole USD 2 outcome. The USD 3 loss already uses 2% of the 5%, so only part of the USD 2 outcome fits.
Forgot the 2% already taken by the worst outcome and filled the entire tail with USD 2 losses.

takeaway: Fill the tail from the worst outcome down and cut the last outcome off at the tail boundary. Here ES = 2.40, not the 2.20 you get by using all of the 8%.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: A final value $X$ lies between 0 and 10 with CDF $F(x) = x^3/1000$. To get the 95% ES you first need the 5% quantile $q$, where $F(q) = 0.05$.
ask: The 5% quantile $q$ is closest to:

options.why: Treated $X$ as uniform on $[0, 10]$, so 5% of the range gives 0.5. The density rises as $x^2$, so far less than that sits near the bottom.
Solved $x^2 = 50$ with a square root instead of the cube root that the cubic CDF needs.

takeaway: Invert the CDF with the right root: $q = 50^{1/3} = 3.68$. The TCE is 2.76, so ES relative to the mean of 7.5 is 4.74.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: The 5% tail is cut into 10 equal slices. The nine interior VaRs (95.5% to 99.5%) sum to 180.05, which averages 20.01. The tail threshold itself, the 95.0% VaR, is 6.33, the lowest of the ten.
ask: If you also averaged in the 95.0% VaR (ten values), the ES estimate would be:

options.label: Higher than 20.01
options.why: Assumed that adding another VaR from the tail can only raise the average. The new value is far below the others.

options.label: The same as 20.01
options.why: Assumed the boundary VaR carries no weight. It does: it adds a low value to the sum and one more to the count.

takeaway: The 95.0% VaR is the edge of the tail, not a slice boundary inside it. Averaging only the $n-1$ interior VaRs avoids dragging the estimate down.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Daily returns are normal with mean +1.0% and standard deviation 5.0%. At 97.5% the tail multiplier is 2.338, so $\sigma \times 2.338 = 11.69\%$ before any adjustment for the mean.
ask: The daily 97.5% ES, quoted as a positive loss, is:

options.label: Above 11.69%
options.why: Added the +1.0% mean to the loss. A positive mean return offsets losses, so it comes off: $11.69 + 1.0 = 12.69$ is the wrong sign.

options.label: Exactly 11.69%
options.why: Dropped the mean entirely. With a positive drift, the tail loss is smaller than the pure volatility term.

takeaway: In loss-positive terms, ES $= -\mu_{\text{return}} + \sigma \times \text{multiplier}$. A positive return mean lowers it.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Three independent bonds, each USD 100 face value, priced at par, with a 10% default probability and zero recovery. The loss is 0, 100, 200 or 300 with probabilities 72.9%, 24.3%, 2.7% and 0.1%. The 95% VaR is USD 100, because a loss of 200 or more has only 2.8% probability.
ask: The 95% expected shortfall is:

options.label: Exactly USD 100
options.why: Equated ES with the VaR. The tail also holds the 2.8% of outcomes at USD 200 or more, which pull the average above the VaR.

options.label: Above USD 200
options.why: Averaged only the outcomes beyond VaR, $(0.1\%\times300 + 2.7\%\times200)/2.8\% = 207$. The tail has 5% mass, so 2.2% must be filled from the USD 100 outcome.

takeaway: With lumpy losses, fill the 5% tail from the worst outcome down and cut the last piece. ES (158) sits above the VaR (100) and well below the worst loss.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Historical simulation with 100 daily P&L observations. The six worst losses are USD 14, 11, 9, 8, 7 and 6m. At 95% the tail holds the worst five; the sixth is the VaR cut-off and is not averaged in.
ask: The one-day 95% ES is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.49m
options.why: Divided the sum of the five tail losses (49) by all 100 observations instead of by the 5 in the tail.

options.label: ≈ USD 49m
options.why: Added the five tail losses and forgot to divide by 5.

options.label: ≈ USD 980m
options.why: Divided the sum by the tail probability 0.05 instead of by the tail count 5.

takeaway: ES is an average: divide by the number of tail observations (5), not by 100 and not by 0.05.

reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
setup: Company A and Company B have cumulative 5-year default probabilities of 10% and 15%. A Gaussian copula with correlation +0.25 links them. If they were independent, the joint default probability would be $10\% \times 15\% = 1.5\%$.
ask: The copula joint 5-year default probability lies:

options.label: Below 1.5%
options.why: Applied positive correlation in the wrong direction. Positive correlation makes joint default more likely than independence.

options.label: Above 10%
options.why: Forgot the ceiling: both companies cannot default together more often than the safer one defaults alone (10%).

takeaway: Positive correlation lifts the joint PD above the product of the PDs; the smaller marginal PD caps it. The copula answer is 2.7%.

reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
setup: Two assets have one-year default probabilities of 5.0% and 7.0%. A Gaussian copula with correlation 0.30 gives the joint default probability from the bivariate normal CDF of the two default thresholds.
ask: The joint one-year default probability is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two probabilities as decimals, $0.05 \times 0.07 = 0.0035$, then read that decimal as a percentage.
Assumed independence: $5\% \times 7\% = 0.35\%$. Correlation of 0.30 lifts the joint probability above that.
Assumed perfect dependence, where joint default equals the smaller PD.

takeaway: A correlation of 0.30 roughly multiplies the independent joint PD by 2.7 here, giving 0.93% against 0.35%. It stays far below the 5% ceiling.

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: A monthly lognormal rate tree has up-node $r_0 e^{\lambda\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{dt}}$ with $r_0 = 2.00\%$, drift $\lambda = 0.50\%$ a year, volatility $\sigma = 9.00\%$ a year and $dt = 1/12$.
ask: The exponent $\lambda\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{dt}$ is closest to:

options.why: Kept only the drift term, $0.005/12$, and dropped the volatility term.
Used $\sigma$ itself and forgot to scale it by $\sqrt{dt}$, a monthly step.
Multiplied $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{12}$ instead of dividing: $0.09 \times 3.46$.

takeaway: Scale volatility by $\sqrt{dt}$, not by $dt$ and not by $\sqrt{1/dt}$. Over one month the shock term (0.026) dwarfs the drift (0.0004).

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: A CIR model $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$ takes monthly steps. The current rate is $r = 2.11\%$, volatility $\sigma = 3.17\%$, and the realised $dw = 0.160$ is already scaled for the time step.
ask: The shock term $\sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$ is closest to:

options.why: Used $r$ instead of $\sqrt{r}$ in the shock: $3.17\% \times 0.0211 \times 0.160$.
Dropped the realised $dw = 0.160$, leaving $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ alone.
Entered $\sigma$ as 3.17 rather than 3.17%, a percent-as-decimal slip that inflates the shock by 100.

takeaway: The shock is $\sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$: take the square root of the rate as a decimal, use $\sigma$ as a percent, and apply the realised $dw$.

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: A CIR step $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$ with $r = 1.00\%$, $\theta = 8.00\%$, $k = 0.60$, $\sigma = 2.5\%$, $dt = 1/12$ and a realised $dw = 0.160$ (already scaled).
ask: Which term dominates the one-month change $dr$?

options.label: The drift term, by about nine times
The shock term
options.why: Took $\sqrt{r} = \sqrt{1.00}$ with $r$ in percent. The formula needs the decimal rate, $\sqrt{0.01} = 0.1$, which cuts the shock to 0.04%.

options.label: They are about equal
options.why: Compared 0.35 with a shock misread at 0.40 and called them similar. The true shock is 0.04%.

takeaway: Use the decimal rate inside $\sqrt{r}$. At low rates $\sqrt{r}$ is small, so the mean-reversion drift can dominate the shock.

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: CIR with monthly steps: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$. The rate is 7.00%, above its long-run level $\theta = 5.00\%$, with $k = 0.30$ and $\sigma = 1.30\%$. Next month brings a shock of +2 standard deviations, $dw = 2\sqrt{1/12} = 0.577$.
ask: Next month the rate most likely:

options.label: Falls, because the rate is above $\theta$
options.why: Looked only at mean reversion, $0.30 \times (5 - 7)/12 = -0.05\%$. The +2 standard-deviation shock adds about +0.20%, which outweighs it.

takeaway: Mean reversion is a gentle pull each month; a 2-sigma shock can overwhelm it. Always compute both terms before calling the sign.

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: A lognormal rate model has $\ln r_1 = \ln r_0 + \alpha\,dt \pm \sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with $r_0 = 5.00\%$, $\alpha = 0.02$, $\sigma = 0.15$ and $dt = 1$.
ask: The lower node after one period is:

options.label: Above 5.00%
options.why: Assumed the positive drift lifts both nodes. The lower node subtracts $\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 0.15$ from a drift of only 0.02, so the exponent is $-0.13$.

takeaway: In a lognormal tree the nodes are $r_0 e^{\alpha dt \pm \sigma\sqrt{dt}}$. When volatility exceeds the drift, the lower node sits below the starting rate.

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: A lognormal model with mean reversion has $d\ln r = k[\ln\theta - \ln r]\,dt$ once volatility is ignored. Here $k = 0.25$ a year, $\theta = 6.00\%$, the current rate is $r = 4.00\%$ and $dt = 1$.
ask: The expected change in $\ln r$ over the year is closest to:

options.why: Used rate differences, $0.25 \times (0.06 - 0.04)$, instead of differences of logs.
Forgot the speed $k$, so the full log gap $\ln(0.06/0.04) = 0.405$ is applied.

takeaway: In log models the pull toward $\theta$ works on $\ln\theta - \ln r$, not on $\theta - r$. Multiply the log gap by $k\,dt$.

reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
setup: In the Gauss+ model the long-term factor decays as $l(t) - \mu = (l(0) - \mu)e^{-\alpha_l t}$. Regressing $\ln|l(t) - \mu|$ on time in years gives a slope of $-0.015$ per year.
ask: The half-life of the deviation, in years, is closest to:

options.why: Reported the regression slope itself instead of a time.
Took $\ln 2 = 0.693$ and forgot to divide by $\alpha_l$.
Scale slip (10×): used $\alpha_l = 0.0015$, a decimal-place error in the slope.

takeaway: Half-life $= \ln 2/\alpha$. A slow speed of 0.015 a year means decay takes decades: about 46 years to halve a deviation.

reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
setup: In a simplified Gauss+ estimation, regressing weekly changes in the 1-year yield on weekly changes in the short rate gives a slope of 0.8625. The model says that sensitivity at maturity $T$ is $e^{-\alpha_r T}$, and $T = 1$.
ask: The mean-reversion speed $\alpha_r$ is closest to:

options.label: −0.15 per year
options.why: Forgot the minus sign in $\alpha_r = -\ln(0.8625)$. The log is negative, so $\alpha_r$ is positive.

options.label: 0.86 per year
options.why: Took the regression slope itself as the speed instead of solving $e^{-\alpha_r} = 0.8625$.

takeaway: A sensitivity below 1 means $\alpha_r > 0$. Take the minus log, and do not read the slope as the speed.

reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
setup: A trader plots a volatility smile for European options with the call delta, instead of the strike, on the x-axis. The axis is arranged so that strikes rise from left to right.
ask: Moving left to right, the call deltas:

options.label: Rise, from near 0.1 to near 0.9
options.why: Reversed the link between strike and delta. A higher strike makes a call less in the money, so its delta falls.

options.label: Rise to 0.5 and then fall
options.why: Mixed up the 25-50-25 shorthand with an actual axis. Call delta is monotone in strike; it does not peak at the money.

working.label: Low strike
working.display: The call is deep in the money, so delta is near its maximum

working.label: High strike
working.display: The call is far out of the money, so delta is near zero

takeaway: Call delta falls monotonically as the strike rises. The 25-50-25 label is shorthand for a 25-delta put, a 50-delta and a 25-delta call.

reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
setup: Linear interpolation on a volatility table in the strike-to-spot ratio $K/S_0$. The grid has columns at 1.00 and 1.05, and the target is $K/S_0 = 1.04$.
ask: The interpolation weight on the 1.05 column is:

options.why: Put the weight on the wrong end. 1.04 is closer to 1.05, so the 1.05 column gets the larger weight.
Used the midpoint of the interval. 1.04 is not halfway between 1.00 and 1.05.
Used the raw distance $1.04 - 1.00$ without dividing by the grid spacing 0.05.

takeaway: The weight on the upper grid point is (target − lower)/(upper − lower). The nearer point always gets the larger weight.

reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
setup: Interpolating a volatility surface for an 11-month option at $K/S_0 = 0.98$. The strike interpolation has already given 13.20% on the 6-month row and 13.92% on the 1-year row.
ask: The final 11-month volatility is:

options.label: Closer to the 6-month value, 13.20%
options.why: Put the weight on the wrong end. 11 months is 5/6 of the way from 6 months to 12 months, so the 1-year row gets the larger weight.

options.label: Midway, 13.56%
options.why: Used the midpoint of the rows. The midpoint maturity is 9 months, not 11.

takeaway: In the time dimension the weights come from the maturity gap too: 11 months lies near 12, so the answer lands near the 1-year row.
